questions.stem: Real GDP differs from nominal GDP because real GDP:
options: adds the value of unpaid household work and volunteering to measured output
leaves out the output of government and other non-market producers
removes the effect of price changes by valuing output at constant prices
removes the effect of population growth by dividing output by population
questions.explanation: Real GDP values output at the prices of a base year, so it changes only when the volume of output changes. Dividing by population gives GDP per capita, which is a different adjustment.

questions.stem: Nominal GDP rose by 5.8% in a year while the general price level, measured by the GDP deflator, rose by 3.1%. Real GDP growth was approximately:
questions.explanation: Real growth is approximately nominal growth minus inflation: 5.8 - 3.1 = 2.7%. Adding the two figures, or reporting the nominal rate, ignores the part of the rise that was only higher prices.

questions.stem: Nominal GDP is $2,640 billion and the GDP price deflator is 120 (base year = 100). Real GDP, in base-year prices, is:
options: $3,168 billion
$2,520 billion
$2,640 billion
$2,200 billion
questions.explanation: Real GDP = nominal GDP / deflator x 100 = 2,640 / 120 x 100 = $2,200 billion. Multiplying by 1.2 instead of dividing inflates the figure rather than removing the price rise.

questions.stem: Why do economists compare output across years using real GDP rather than nominal GDP?
options: Nominal GDP leaves out exports, so it understates output in trade-heavy years
Real GDP counts only private sector output, which is measured more reliably
Real GDP is adjusted for population, so it shows output per person directly
Nominal GDP can rise purely because prices rise, even if output does not
questions.explanation: Nominal GDP mixes changes in quantity with changes in price, so inflation alone can make it grow. Real GDP strips out price changes; it is not adjusted for population, which is what GDP per capita does.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of GDP as a measure of living standards?
options: It does not show how income is distributed among households
It counts intermediate goods again at each stage of production
It leaves out government spending on goods and services
It leaves out the value of goods sold to other countries
questions.explanation: GDP is a total, so the same figure is consistent with very equal or very unequal incomes. GDP is built from final output or value added, so intermediate goods are not double counted, and it includes government spending and exports.

questions.stem: A parent leaves paid work to care full-time for their young child at home. Measured GDP falls, although useful work is still being done. This illustrates GDP's exclusion of:
options: the non-market sector
the informal economy
environmental degradation
hours worked
questions.explanation: Unpaid work in the home, such as childcare and cooking, is non-market production that GDP does not count. The informal economy is paid work that goes unreported, such as cash jobs, which is a different gap in the data.

questions.stem: A tradesperson does weekend jobs for cash and does not declare the income. GDP is understated because of:
options: the non-market sector
depletion of the resource base
the distribution of income
the informal economy
questions.explanation: Paid activity that is hidden from the tax and statistics agencies forms the informal (cash or shadow) economy, so it is missed from GDP. The non-market sector is unpaid production, such as volunteering.

questions.stem: In a country with a stable population, real GDP rises by 3% in a year while total hours worked rise by 6%. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Output per hour worked fell, so the growth came partly at the cost of leisure
Wellbeing clearly rose, because real output per person increased
Labour productivity rose, because both output and hours increased
Real GDP per person must have fallen during the year
questions.explanation: Output grew more slowly than hours, so output per hour fell and people gave up leisure to produce more. GDP ignores the value of leisure, which is why it can overstate the gain in wellbeing. Real GDP per person did rise, as population was stable.

questions.stem: A logging boom clears old-growth forest and raises GDP this year. Why may GDP overstate the gain in wellbeing?
options: It counts the timber output but not the loss of a natural asset
It counts the timber twice, once when felled and again when sold
It leaves out timber that is sold overseas from measured output
It records only the loggers' wages and not the value of the timber
questions.explanation: GDP adds the value of the timber but makes no deduction for depleting the resource base or degrading the environment. Timber exports are part of GDP, and value added is counted only once.

questions.stem: Real GDP grows by 1.5% in a year while the population grows by 2.2%. Real GDP per capita:
options: rose by about 3.7%
was unchanged, as output grew
fell by about 0.7%
rose by about 0.7%
questions.explanation: Growth in real GDP per capita is approximately real GDP growth minus population growth: 1.5 - 2.2 = -0.7%. Total output rose, but it was shared among proportionally more people.

questions.stem: A technical recession is usually defined as:
options: a single quarter in which real GDP growth slows down
two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth
two consecutive quarters of falling nominal GDP
a year in which the unemployment rate rises sharply
questions.explanation: The common rule of thumb is two quarters in a row in which real GDP falls. Nominal GDP can fall simply because prices fall, and a slowdown in growth is not a fall in output.

questions.stem: A per capita recession occurs when:
options: total real GDP falls for two consecutive quarters while the population is steady
nominal GDP per person falls because the general price level is declining
real GDP growth is positive but below its long-run average rate for a year
real GDP per person falls for two consecutive quarters, even if total real GDP rises
questions.explanation: If population grows faster than output, output per person falls even while total real GDP rises. Australia has had per capita recessions in periods of strong population growth without a technical recession.

questions.stem: Compared with a recession, a depression is:
options: a much deeper and more prolonged fall in output, with very high unemployment
a short, mild slowdown in which growth stays positive but below its trend rate
a fall in the general price level that lasts for two or more quarters
a period of rising output combined with rapidly rising inflation
questions.explanation: A depression is a severe and long-lasting contraction, such as the Great Depression of the 1930s, when unemployment reached very high levels. A falling price level is deflation, not a depression.

questions.stem: Quarterly real GDP growth is: Q1 +0.4%, Q2 -0.2%, Q3 +0.1%, Q4 -0.3%. Population grows by 0.5% each quarter. Which statement is correct?
options: There was a technical recession, because real GDP fell in two quarters
There was neither a technical recession nor a per capita recession
There was a technical recession but no per capita recession
There was no technical recession, but there was a per capita recession
questions.explanation: Real GDP never fell in two consecutive quarters, so there was no technical recession. Per capita growth was about -0.7%, -0.4% and -0.8% in Q2 to Q4, which are consecutive falls in output per person.

questions.stem: Aggregate supply is:
options: the total quantity of goods and services producers are willing and able to supply at each price level
the total spending on goods and services by households, businesses, government and overseas buyers
the amount of output the economy produces when the unemployment rate is zero
the total value of imports supplied to the domestic economy over a full year by foreign producers
questions.explanation: Aggregate supply relates the economy's total planned output to the price level. Total spending is aggregate demand, the other side of the AD-AS model.

questions.stem: Which change would increase Australia's aggregate supply?
options: A rise in the price level caused by stronger demand
A rise in labour productivity from wider use of automation
A rise in household spending after a cut in income tax
A rise in the cash rate to slow the pace of inflation
questions.explanation: Higher productivity lets the economy produce more from the same inputs, shifting AS to the right. Tax cuts raise aggregate demand, and a change in the price level is a movement along AS rather than a shift.

questions.stem: An increase in the quality of labour inputs would most likely come from:
options: employees working more hours each week in their existing jobs
a larger working-age population through higher immigration
a fall in the price of imported machinery and equipment
more workers completing apprenticeships and tertiary qualifications
questions.explanation: Education and training raise the skills, and so the quality, of labour. Longer hours and a larger population raise the quantity of labour, and cheaper machinery affects capital.

questions.stem: Which factor mainly increases the quantity of inputs available to the economy?
options: Improved skills of existing workers through training
Higher net overseas migration of working-age people
Better management practices within existing businesses
Wider use of digital tools by the current workforce
questions.explanation: Migration adds workers, a larger quantity of labour. Better management, technology and training make existing inputs more productive or of higher quality, rather than adding more of them.

questions.stem: Potential output is:
options: the real GDP the economy can produce when resources are fully employed without rising inflation
the highest level of real GDP that the economy has ever recorded in a single year
the level of real GDP forecast by Treasury for the coming financial year
the level of real GDP at which every member of the labour force has a job
questions.explanation: Potential output is the sustainable level of production when labour and capital are fully employed, which still allows some frictional and structural unemployment. It is not zero unemployment.

questions.stem: When actual output is below potential output, the economy is most likely to have:
options: full employment, because some unemployment always exists anyway
rising inflation, as firms raise prices to cover their idle capacity
a negative output gap, with spare capacity and cyclical unemployment
a positive output gap, with capacity constraints and rising inflation
questions.explanation: Output below potential means resources are idle, so cyclical unemployment rises and inflation pressure eases. A positive output gap is the opposite case, when output runs above potential.

questions.stem: Actual output has been above potential output for several quarters. Which outcome is most likely?
options: A widening negative output gap as business investment slows
Rising inflation pressure as firms struggle to keep up with demand
Rising cyclical unemployment as firms run below their capacity
A falling price level as spare capacity builds up across the economy
questions.explanation: Output can exceed potential only by stretching resources, which pushes up wages and prices. Cyclical unemployment and spare capacity belong to a negative output gap.

questions.stem: On an AD-AS graph, a rise in business investment spending, with nothing else changing, is shown as:
options: AS shifting right, raising real GDP and lowering the price level
AD shifting left, lowering real GDP and the price level
a movement along AD to higher real GDP at a lower price level
AD shifting right, raising real GDP and the price level
questions.explanation: Investment is a component of aggregate demand, so more of it shifts AD right, raising output and the price level. In the long run the new capital may also add to AS, but the immediate effect is on demand.

questions.stem: On an AD-AS graph, a sustained rise in productivity across the economy is shown as:
options: a movement up along the AS curve to a higher price level
a rightward shift of AS, raising real GDP and easing the price level
a rightward shift of AD, raising both real GDP and the price level
a leftward shift of AS, lowering real GDP and raising the price level
questions.explanation: Higher productivity lowers costs per unit of output, so producers supply more at each price level and AS shifts right. Output rises while pressure on prices falls.

questions.stem: A severe drought cuts farm output while consumer confidence falls sharply at the same time. Using the AD-AS model, the effect is:
options: real GDP falls and the price level clearly rises
real GDP rises and the price level clearly falls
the change in real GDP is uncertain, while the price level rises
real GDP falls, but the change in the price level is uncertain
questions.explanation: The drought shifts AS left (output down, prices up) and weaker confidence shifts AD left (output down, prices down). Both lower real GDP, but they push the price level in opposite directions, so its change depends on the sizes of the shifts.

questions.stem: Under the AD-AS model, which combination of shifts would raise real GDP without raising the price level?
options: AD and AS both shift right by similar amounts
AD shifts right while AS shifts left
AD shifts left while AS is unchanged
AS shifts left while AD is unchanged
questions.explanation: When AS grows as fast as AD, output rises while the price level stays about the same: non-inflationary growth. AD rising alone would lift prices, and a leftward AS shift lowers output.

questions.stem: Strong economic growth generally benefits households by:
options: creating jobs and raising real incomes
lowering the general price level each year
removing the need for households to save
guaranteeing an equal distribution of income
questions.explanation: Growing output means businesses hire more workers and incomes rise. Growth does not lower prices or ensure equal distribution of the gains.

questions.stem: How does a period of economic decline affect the government's budget?
options: Welfare spending falls as fewer people qualify, improving the balance
Tax revenue falls and welfare spending rises, worsening the budget balance
Tax revenue rises and welfare spending falls, improving the budget balance
Tax revenue and welfare spending both fall, leaving the balance unchanged
questions.explanation: With lower incomes and profits, tax collections fall, while more people receive unemployment and other payments. These automatic stabilisers push the budget towards deficit.

questions.stem: During a period of strong economic growth, a business is most likely to:
options: cut prices sharply to clear unsold stock
reduce staff hours as sales fall away
postpone expansion as confidence falls
invest in new capital to meet rising demand
questions.explanation: Rising sales and confidence encourage firms to expand capacity by investing in equipment and buildings. Discounting to clear stock and cutting hours are typical of a downturn.

questions.stem: A cost of very rapid economic growth is that it can:
options: reduce tax revenue and push the budget further into deficit each year
cause the price level to fall as supply grows faster than demand
add to inflation and environmental pressure if it outpaces productive capacity
raise cyclical unemployment as firms cut production and lay off staff
questions.explanation: Growth faster than capacity creates inflation, and faster production also uses more resources and creates more pollution. Rising cyclical unemployment and falling tax revenue are features of decline, not growth.

questions.stem: Australia's recession in 2020 was triggered mainly by:
options: a sharp rise in the cash rate to bring down very high inflation
a collapse in the world price of wool at the end of a long boom
a crash in the share market following a long period of speculation
health restrictions that shut down activity during the COVID-19 pandemic
questions.explanation: Real GDP fell in the March and June quarters of 2020 as lockdowns and border closures halted activity. High interest rates were a major cause of the early 1990s recession, not of the 2020 one.

questions.stem: Before 2020, Australia's previous recession was in:
options: the late 2000s, during the global financial crisis
the early 2000s, after the dot-com crash
the mid-1980s, after the dollar was floated
the early 1990s
questions.explanation: Australia's last recession before 2020 was in 1990-91. It avoided a recession during the global financial crisis, helped by large stimulus, interest rate cuts and demand for resources from China.

questions.stem: Australia's real GDP growth in the 2000s and early 2010s was strongly supported by:
options: a fall in the terms of trade that lifted export volumes
a resources boom driven by strong demand from China
a sharp rise in manufacturing exports to Europe
a long period of falling population and migration
questions.explanation: Rapid industrialisation in China raised prices and volumes for Australian iron ore, coal and gas, lifting incomes and mining investment. The terms of trade rose, rather than fell, during the boom.

questions.stem: In some periods Australia's total real GDP growth has held up while growth in real GDP per capita has been weak. Which factor best explains weak per capita growth?
options: slow growth in labour productivity
rapid growth in the size of the labour force
a rising participation rate among older workers
strong growth in the economy's capital stock
questions.explanation: Lasting growth in output per person depends mainly on productivity. A growing labour force lifts total GDP but not necessarily GDP per person, and higher participation or more capital per worker would tend to raise output per person.

questions.stem: A table shows real GDP of $2,000 billion in Year 1, $2,060 billion in Year 2 and $2,039.4 billion in Year 3. Real GDP growth in Year 3 was:
questions.explanation: Growth in Year 3 = (2,039.4 - 2,060) / 2,060 x 100 = -1.0%. The 3.0% figure is Year 2's growth, and 1.97% is the change over both years from Year 1.

questions.stem: A time-series line graph shows Australia's annual real GDP growth falling from 3% to 1% over two years while staying above zero. Which statement is correct?
options: Real GDP kept rising, but at a slower rate
Real GDP fell, because the growth rate fell
The economy entered a technical recession
The price level must have fallen over the period
questions.explanation: A positive growth rate means output is still increasing, so a falling but positive rate shows slower growth, not decline. Output falls only when the growth rate is negative.

questions.stem: The long-run average rate at which real GDP grows is called:
options: the business cycle peak
the trend rate of growth
the output gap
the nominal rate of growth
questions.explanation: The trend rate smooths out the ups and downs of the business cycle. The output gap measures how far actual output is from potential at a point in time.

questions.stem: Two countries each record 3% real GDP growth. Country A's population grows by 1% and Country B's by 2.5%. Which statement is correct?
options: Real GDP per capita rose by more in Country A
Real GDP per capita rose by more in Country B
Real GDP per capita rose equally in both countries
Real GDP per capita fell in Country B
questions.explanation: Per capita growth is about 3 - 1 = 2% in A and 3 - 2.5 = 0.5% in B. Both rose, but output per person grew much faster in A.
